SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE.
REPORT

SHAI MUNICIPAL PO...
S. B. REGISTRY
File No. S. B. D. 7145
S.I., Special Branch Series,
Date December 4, 1935.

Subject Activities of students of local schools in connection
with political situation

Made by D.I. Sh Tse-liang Forwarded by [签名]

Discreet enquiries have been made with a view to
bringing to light any agitation existing among students of
local schools in connection with the recent developments in
the Sino-Japanese Situation, but so far no information worthy
of note has come to light.

Confidential information reveals that the Chinese
students of local schools pay little attention to current
political affairs in consequence of the strict surveillance
exercised by the Chinese Authorities.

Following the conclusion of the peace agreement between
the local Chinese Authorities and the Japanese Military
officials subsequent to the Sino-Japanese hostilities in
Chapel in 1932, students of local schools lost interest in
politics, and organizations of political trend in schools
disappeared one after another. Nevertheless the occupation
of Jehol and the movement inside the Great Wall of Japanese
troops at the beginning of 1933 re-kindled to some extent the
ardour of the students. Students' Volunteer armies were
organized and funds raised for the relief of the troops engaged
in resisting the Japanese. Attempts were made by local
students to resuscitate, under the supervision of the local
Kuomintang, the defunct University Students' Federation and
the Middle School Students' Federation, which played a leading
part in the students' activities in 1931. The attempts
to revive these organizations ceased in the middle of May, 1933,
when, following the signing of the Tanku Pact between the
Japanese and Chinese on May 31, 1933, students' activities
of an anti-Japanese nature were prohibited by the Chinese
Authorities.

（印：DEPUTY COMMISSIONER 5 DEC. 1935 CRIME BRANCH）
（印：OFFICE OF COMMISSIONER OF POLICE 6 DEC. ... SHANGHAI）
（批：S.I, Please bring up to date...）

Since that time the authorities have paid close attention
to the activities of Chinese students, and it is believed that
the local Kuomintang has placed agents in the Chinese schools
to forestall any reactionary activities.

The majority of the students who played important roles
in the anti-Japanese movement in 1931, have graduated, and
departed from Shanghai. Consequently, no organizations of any
political significance are now in existence, and, with the
strict surveillance now exercised by the Chinese Authorities,
it is unlikely that such organizations will be allowed to come
into existence.

In the three municipalities of Shanghai there are at
present some twenty universities and colleges, eighty middle
schools, and 1,000 primary schools, all of which are under the
control or supervision of the Chinese Authorities.

Attached herewith is a list of schools, the students
of which have participated in political movements during the
past few years.

Agent Yao Gee-chong assisted in obtaining information
for the compilation of this report.

Sih Tse Liang
D. I.
D.C. (Special Branch).
S.L. (Crime)

POLICE FORCE.
MUNICIPAL COUNCIL
C. D. Smith Shanghai, November 24 1935
To S. I.

Please report on
extent to which various
schools in Shanghai
have been affected by
agitation recently and
the nature of the agitation.
In compiling the report and
collecting information, please
give special attention to
schools, such as the Fine
Arts College, French Town,
and branches of Fuh Tan
College which was formerly
notorious for agitation among
their students. JWS

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE.
Section 2, Special Branch
REPORT
File No. MUNICIPAL POLICE
S.I. REGIST.
Date December 4, 19 35.
Subject Enquiries re. anti-Japanese activities.
Made by D.S.I. Coyne Forwarded by
I have to report that on the instructions of the
Deputy Commissioner (Special Branch) enquiries were made by
detectives and agents, working in the sections shown in the
attached plan, regarding possible anti-Japanese activities.
The schools shown on the attached list were visited
with a view to ascertaining whether meetings of a political
nature have been held recently, or any political organization
has been formed. Nothing was learned however which would
indicate that students of any of these schools were in any
way concerned in the attack of the premises of Messrs. Hibino
Yoko, or members of an anti-Japanese organization.
Enquiries made at industrial concerns in that area also
failed to elicit information which would indicate that an
organized anti-Japanese movement was afoot.
J. Coyne
D. S. I.
Deputy Commissioner (Special Branch).
SI.
Please let me know the result
of your inquiries about schools in
general.
J.W.S.
4/12/35
